textbookText: Figure 2.8.5 Morphology of a typical leaf A typical leaf consists of three main parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina. The leaves are attached to stem by leaf base and may bear lateral small leaf like structures called stipules. The leaf having stipule is called stipulate and leaf without stipule is called exstipulate. The petiole is the stalk of leaf that holds the blade to light. It connects the lamina with branch of stem. The leaf with petiole is called petiolate leaf while the leaf without petiole is called sessile leaf. The lamina or the leaf blade is the green flattened part of the leaf with network of veins. The lamina is the most important part of the leaf since this is the site of food manufacture for the whole plant. The vein that runs from petiole to the apex is called as mid rib or main vein. The mid rib produces thinner lateral veins which further give rise to veinlets.

The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina of leaf is called as venation. When the veinlets form a network, the venation is called reticulate venation (e.g. leaves of dicot plant). When the veins run parallel to each other within a lamina, the venation is called as parallel venation (e.g. leaves of monocot plant).

Figure 2.8.6 Venation (a) Reticulate venation (b) Parallel venation Types of leaf A leaf which may be entire or incised to any depth but not down to the midrib or petiole is simple leaf. When the incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib breaking it into a number of leaflets, the leaf is called compound leaf. The compound leaves are of two types i.e. pinnately Biology, Grade 11 | 151
compound leaf (number of leaflets are present on a common axis) and palmately compound leaf (leaflets are attached at a common point).

Figure 2.8.7 Types of leaf (a) Simple leaf (b) Compound leaf Phyllotaxy Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on a stem or branch. The leaves are so arranged that they get appropriate amount of sunlight for photosynthesis. It avoids overcrowding of leaves at one place. It is basically of three types: alternate, opposite and whorled as shown below in the diagram.

Figure 2.8.8 Arrangement of leaf Functions of leaf: i. The main function of leaf is to manufacture food during the process of photosynthesis. ii. It helps in exchange of gases between atmosphere and the plant body. iii. It helps in transpiration i.e. removal of excess of water in the form of vapour from the aerial part of the plant. iv. Some modified leaves help to store the food. v. The leaves of Bryophyllum, Begonia etc. produce buds on their margin that develop into new plants. vi. The leaves provide protection to axillary bud.
4. THE INFLORESCENCE The axis that bears flowers is called peduncle. Inflorescence is defined as the
arrangement of flowers on floral axis or peduncle.
Depending on whether the floral axis terminates into a flower or shows continuous growth, the inflorescences are of two types:

a. Racemose: In this type of inflorescence the main axis continues to grow and does not terminate in a flower. The flowers are developed laterally in acropetal manner (i.e. older flowers are arranged towards base and young flowers at tip) or centripetal manner (i.e. younger flowers are arranged at centre and older flowers are arranged in periphery).

b. Cymose: In this type of inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower. The further growth occurs from nearby lateral branches which also end in flowers. The flower are developed in a basipetal order (i.e. the older flowers are present at tip and young buds are arranged towards base). 5. THE FLOWER Flower is a highly condensed and modified reproductive shoot. It is meant for sexual reproduction. The study of flower is called anthology. Bracts are modified reduced leaves present at the base of some flower. The flower with bract is called bracteate flower and the flower without bract is called ebracteate flower. The flower has short or long stalk known as pedicel. Flower with pedicel is called pedicellate but without pedicel is called sessile. The upper part of pedicel is swollen, spherical or conical in shape which is called thalamus or receptacle.
2.8.10 Structure of a typical flower Symmetry of flower The floral symmetry may be actinomorphic (radially symmetry), zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry) or asymmetric (irregular).
